questions.stem: Bharat Heavy Fabricators Ltd's engineering division builds a specialised furnace for the company's own production division, working to an internally negotiated design over two accounting years. Under AS 7 the arrangement is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — AS 7 applies in the financial statements of contractors; two parties needed

readLink.label: Read: Whose books, and why a special standard, §1 →

options.text: Within AS 7, because the asset is specifically negotiated and takes more than one accounting year
options.explanation: Specific negotiation and a multi-year build are features of a construction contract, but they cannot supply the missing second party — an enterprise earns nothing by dealing with itself.

options.text: Within AS 7, with the production division treated as the contractee at an agreed internal transfer price
options.explanation: An internal transfer price does not create a customer; inter-divisional charges are eliminated within one set of financial statements.

options.text: Within AS 7 only if the furnace is a combination of closely interrelated assets
options.explanation: The interrelated-assets limb only widens what counts as the asset once a contract with a customer exists; it does not turn an internal build into a contract.

options.text: Outside AS 7 — a construction contract needs a contractor and a customer, so the furnace is a self-constructed asset accounted for under AS 10
options.explanation: Correct. AS 7 governs accounting in the financial statements of contractors, with the customer as contractee; one division cannot be the other's customer, so the furnace is a self-constructed fixed asset measured under AS 10.

questions.stem: Which of the following falls within the scope of AS 7?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — contracts for services directly related to construction and for destruction/restoration

readLink.label: Read: Whose books, and why a special standard, §1 →

options.text: The sale of a completed flat from a builder's unsold finished stock
options.explanation: Nothing remains to be constructed for that buyer; a completed unit sold out of stock is an ordinary sale of goods under AS 9.

options.text: A contract to supply cement to a road contractor at an agreed rate per tonne
options.explanation: The supplier constructs no asset — it sells goods; AS 9 governs its revenue, and the cement is a contract cost in the contractor's books.

options.text: A contract giving a tower crane on hire to a bridge contractor for eighteen months
options.explanation: Hiring out plant is the letting of equipment, not the construction of an asset; the crane owner builds nothing for the hirer.

options.text: A contract with a firm of architects for design and project-management services directly related to the construction of a metro station
options.explanation: Correct. AS 7 covers contracts for services directly related to the construction of an asset — project managers and architects — as well as contracts for the destruction or restoration of assets and of the environment following demolition.

questions.stem: A single contract covers three assets. It may be segmented — each asset treated as a separate construction contract — only when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — three cumulative conditions for segmenting a contract

readLink.label: Read: Segmenting and combining, §1 →

options.text: The three assets are constructed concurrently and each has its own completion date
options.explanation: Concurrent or continuous performance is a test for COMBINING contracts, not for segmenting one; and separate completion dates appear nowhere in the segmenting conditions.

options.text: The customer settles each asset through a separate running account bill
options.explanation: Separate billing is a payment arrangement. Segmenting turns on how the work was proposed and negotiated and on the identifiability of each asset's costs and revenues.

options.text: Each asset can be identified separately in the contractor's fixed asset register
options.explanation: The assets being built belong to the customer, so they never enter the contractor's fixed asset register at all.

options.text: Separate proposals were submitted for each asset, each asset was separately negotiated with the customer free to accept or reject that part, and the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions must hold together: separate proposals, separate negotiation with a genuine accept-or-reject choice on each asset, and identifiable costs and revenues per asset.

questions.stem: Nagavali Constructions Ltd has signed three contracts, with two different customers, for parts of the same petrochemical complex. AS 7 requires them to be accounted for as a single construction contract when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — three cumulative conditions for combining contracts

readLink.label: Read: Segmenting and combining, §1 →

options.text: Each contract taken on its own would report a loss
options.explanation: The expected outcome cannot decide the unit of account — combining depends on the three tests, and any contract that fails them carries its own expected loss in full.

options.text: They were negotiated as a single package, are so closely interrelated that they are in effect part of a single project with an overall profit margin, and are performed concurrently or in a continuous sequence
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions must hold; combining is expressly available whether the contracts are with a single customer or with several.

options.text: They are with the same customer and are performed concurrently
options.explanation: Combining does not require one customer at all, and a common customer plus concurrency is short of the test — the single-package and single-project conditions must also hold.

options.text: Their combined value exceeds the contractor's normal contract size
options.explanation: Contract size is not a criterion anywhere in AS 7; the unit of account follows the negotiation and performance tests.

questions.stem: Midway through a contract the customer orders an additional asset. AS 7 treats it as a SEPARATE construction contract when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — additional asset: either limb suffices

readLink.label: Read: Segmenting and combining, §1 →

options.text: Either the asset differs significantly in design, technology or function from the assets covered by the original contract, or its price is negotiated without regard to the original contract price
options.explanation: Correct. The two limbs are alternatives — satisfying either one makes the additional asset a separate contract.

options.text: Both limbs hold — the asset differs significantly in design, technology or function AND its price is negotiated without regard to the original contract price
options.explanation: This reads the standard's 'or' as 'and'; either limb on its own is enough to separate the additional asset.

options.text: The price of the additional asset exceeds the price of the original contract
options.explanation: Relative value is not a test; what matters is whether the asset differs significantly or was priced independently.

options.text: The additional asset is to be delivered after the original contract is complete
options.explanation: Delivery sequence is irrelevant — an additional asset built concurrently can still be a separate contract if either limb is met.

questions.stem: A contract fixes the price at ₹4,80,000 per kilometre of highway built, and provides that any increase in bitumen prices beyond a stated index will be passed on to the contractor. The contract is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — fixed price includes a fixed rate per unit of output; escalation clauses do not change the category

readLink.label: Read: Fixed price and cost-plus, §1 →

options.text: A cost-plus contract, because no fixed total sum is stated
options.explanation: A fixed rate per unit of output is expressly a fixed price contract even though the total depends on the output achieved.

options.text: Outside AS 7 until the escalation is finally settled with the customer
options.explanation: AS 7 applies from the start of the contract; the escalation simply enters contract revenue once it is probable and reliably measurable.

options.text: A fixed price contract — a fixed rate per unit of output is a fixed price contract, and a cost-escalation clause does not alter that classification
options.explanation: Correct. AS 7 defines a fixed price contract as one for a fixed contract price or a fixed rate per unit of output, in some cases subject to cost-escalation clauses.

options.text: A cost-plus contract, because a part of the contractor's costs is reimbursed by the customer
options.explanation: An escalation clause adjusts an agreed price for a defined input movement. A cost-plus contract reimburses allowable or otherwise defined costs plus a percentage of those costs or a fixed fee.

questions.stem: Netravati Constructions Ltd holds a fixed price contract of ₹1,200 lakh. The escalation clause passes on 40% of any increase in material cost, and material costs have risen ₹50 lakh. The customer has approved a variation worth ₹45 lakh. An early-completion incentive of ₹30 lakh is probable of being earned and can be measured reliably, while a claim of ₹18 lakh for extra approval costs is disputed and its acceptance by the customer is not probable. Contract revenue is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — contract revenue build-up: agreed price + escalation + variation + probable incentive

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract revenue, §1 →

options.text: ₹1,325 lakh
options.explanation: This passes on the whole ₹50 lakh material increase; the clause passes on only 40% of it, that is ₹20 lakh.

options.text: ₹1,295 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. 1,200 + (40% × 50 = 20 escalation) + 45 variation + 30 incentive = ₹1,295 lakh; the ₹18 lakh claim stays out because acceptance is not probable.

options.text: ₹1,313 lakh
options.explanation: This adds the ₹18 lakh disputed claim. A claim enters contract revenue only when it is probable it will result in revenue and the amount is reliably measurable.

options.text: ₹1,265 lakh
options.explanation: This drops the ₹30 lakh incentive, which qualifies on both counts — earning it is probable and it is reliably measurable.

questions.stem: A contractor's claim on the customer for costs not included in the contract price is included in contract revenue when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — claims and incentives: probable + reliably measurable

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract revenue, §1 →

options.text: The contractor is confident of recovery whatever stand the customer takes
options.explanation: The contractor's own optimism is not the test; probability turns on the state of negotiations with the customer, and the amount must also be reliably measurable.

options.text: It is probable that the claim will result in revenue and the amount can be measured reliably
options.explanation: Correct. Variations, claims and incentive payments enter contract revenue only to the extent that it is probable they will result in revenue and they are capable of being measured reliably.

options.text: The claim has been raised on the customer in writing
options.explanation: Raising a claim says nothing about the outcome; recognition waits until the negotiations make revenue probable and the amount measurable.

options.text: The arbitrator has made a final award on the claim
options.explanation: Waiting for a final award is later than AS 7 requires — recognition begins when the outcome is probable and reliably measurable, typically at an advanced stage of negotiation.

questions.stem: Tapti Constructions Ltd has a fixed price contract of ₹600 lakh. The escalation clause passes on 50% of any increase in material cost, and the whole increase in labour cost provided the rise in minimum wages does not exceed 25%. During the year material costs rose ₹36 lakh, and minimum wages rose 20% against an original labour estimate of ₹80 lakh. An incentive of ₹14 lakh is available for early completion, but the contractor is behind schedule and earning it is not probable. Contract revenue is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — escalation clause with a partial pass-through and a wage-rise ceiling

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract revenue, §1 →

options.text: ₹652 lakh
options.explanation: This passes on the entire ₹36 lakh material increase instead of the 50% (₹18 lakh) the clause allows.

options.text: ₹634 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. 600 + (50% × 36 = 18 material escalation) + (the 20% wage rise is within the 25% ceiling, so the whole labour increase passes: 80 × 20% = 16) = ₹634 lakh; the ₹14 lakh incentive is excluded because earning it is not probable.

options.text: ₹618 lakh
options.explanation: This counts only the material escalation. The wage rise of 20% is inside the 25% ceiling, so the labour escalation of ₹16 lakh does pass on.

options.text: ₹648 lakh
options.explanation: This adds the ₹14 lakh incentive; an incentive payment enters contract revenue only when meeting the specified performance standard is probable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is expressly EXCLUDED from contract costs under AS 7?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — costs excluded from contract costs

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract costs, §1 →

options.text: Selling costs
options.explanation: Correct. Selling costs are excluded, along with general administration and research and development costs for which reimbursement is not specified in the contract, and depreciation of idle plant not used on a particular contract.

options.text: Depreciation of plant and equipment used on the contract
options.explanation: Depreciation of plant used on the contract is a direct contract cost — it is only IDLE plant not used on a particular contract whose depreciation is excluded.

options.text: The cost of moving plant and materials to and from the site
options.explanation: Mobilisation and demobilisation costs relate directly to the contract and are included.

options.text: Estimated costs of rectification and guarantee work, including expected warranty costs
options.explanation: These relate directly to the contract and are included as contract costs even though the outflow comes later.

questions.stem: For the year, Bhima Constructions Ltd records against one contract: site labour including supervision ₹180 lakh; materials consumed at the site ₹240 lakh; depreciation of plant used on the contract ₹60 lakh; hire of plant ₹25 lakh; insurance allocable to the contract ₹20 lakh; general administration costs for which the contract specifies no reimbursement ₹28 lakh; selling costs ₹15 lakh; depreciation of idle plant not used on any contract ₹12 lakh; and ₹8 lakh realised by selling surplus materials bought for the contract. Contract costs for the year are:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — direct + allocable costs, incidental income credited, excluded costs

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract costs, §1 →

options.text: ₹572 lakh
options.explanation: This includes all three excluded items — general administration ₹28 lakh, selling costs ₹15 lakh and idle-plant depreciation ₹12 lakh.

options.text: ₹517 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. 180 + 240 + 60 + 25 + 20 = ₹525 lakh, less the ₹8 lakh incidental income from surplus materials = ₹517 lakh; general administration without a reimbursement clause, selling costs and idle-plant depreciation are all excluded.

options.text: ₹525 lakh
options.explanation: This omits the ₹8 lakh from selling surplus materials, which is incidental income not forming part of contract revenue and therefore reduces the direct contract cost.

options.text: ₹545 lakh
options.explanation: This adds back the ₹28 lakh of general administration cost, which enters contract costs only where the contract specifies reimbursement.

questions.stem: Construction overheads that cannot be traced to a single contract are allocated to contracts:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — allocation of construction overheads on normal levels of activity

readLink.label: Read: What goes into contract costs, §1 →

options.text: On the activity level actually achieved in the period, however low it may be
options.explanation: Allocating on an abnormally low actual level would push the cost of idle capacity into contract costs; AS 7 requires normal levels as the base.

options.text: In the ratio of the contract prices of the contracts in hand
options.explanation: Contract price is a revenue measure, not a measure of the construction activity that drives these overheads.

options.text: Not at all — only costs directly traceable to a contract are contract costs
options.explanation: Allocable costs attributable to contract activity in general are the second of the three contract-cost buckets, alongside direct costs and costs specifically chargeable to the customer.

options.text: Systematically and rationally, on the basis of the normal level of construction activity
options.explanation: Correct. Costs attributable to contract activity in general — insurance, non-specific design, construction overheads and AS 16 borrowing costs — are allocated on normal levels of construction activity so that idle capacity is not loaded onto contracts.

questions.stem: A contractor whose contract outcome can be estimated reliably may recognise contract revenue and contract costs using:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — percentage of completion is the only permitted method

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

options.text: The percentage of completion method, unless the contract runs beyond three years
options.explanation: There is no duration cut-off; the trigger is whether the outcome can be estimated reliably.

options.text: Only the percentage of completion method
options.explanation: Correct. AS 7 permits a single method: revenue and costs are recognised by reference to the stage of completion at the reporting date, so that each period carries the result of the work performed in it.

options.text: Either the percentage of completion method or the completed contract method, as a matter of accounting policy
options.explanation: The completed contract method is not an option under AS 7 — it would show cost-heavy loss years followed by one windfall year.

options.text: The completed contract method, with percentage of completion allowed only for cost-plus contracts
options.explanation: The method does not depend on the contract type; percentage of completion applies to fixed price and cost-plus contracts alike once the outcome is reliably estimable.

questions.stem: For a FIXED PRICE construction contract, which of the following is NOT one of the conditions AS 7 requires before the outcome is treated as capable of reliable estimation?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — the four conditions for a fixed price contract

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

options.text: Both the contract costs to complete and the stage of completion at the reporting date can be measured reliably
options.explanation: This is the third condition, and it has two limbs — costs to complete AND stage of completion.

options.text: Contract costs are clearly identifiable and can be measured reliably, so that actual costs can be compared with prior estimates
options.explanation: This is the fourth condition, which makes the estimating process self-correcting.

options.text: The customer has furnished a bank guarantee covering the unbilled portion of the contract price
options.explanation: Correct. There is no security requirement. The four conditions are: total contract revenue can be measured reliably; it is probable the economic benefits will flow to the enterprise; both the costs to complete and the stage of completion at the reporting date can be measured reliably; and contract costs are clearly identifiable and reliably measurable so actual costs can be compared with prior estimates.

options.text: Total contract revenue can be measured reliably
options.explanation: This is the first of the four conditions.

questions.stem: The outcome of a COST-PLUS contract is treated as capable of reliable estimation when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — the two conditions for a cost-plus contract

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

options.text: It is probable that the economic benefits associated with the contract will flow to the enterprise, and the contract costs attributable to the contract — whether or not specifically reimbursable — are clearly identifiable and can be measured reliably
options.explanation: Correct. A cost-plus contract needs only these two conditions; the reimbursement mechanism itself removes the revenue-measurement risk that the other two fixed-price conditions address.

options.text: All four conditions applicable to a fixed price contract are satisfied
options.explanation: That over-states the requirement — the standard prescribes only two conditions for cost-plus contracts.

options.text: The costs specifically reimbursable under the contract can be identified and measured reliably
options.explanation: The condition extends to contract costs attributable to the contract whether or not they are specifically reimbursable, not merely the reimbursable slice.

options.text: The customer has agreed the percentage fee in advance and the contract has run for at least one accounting year
options.explanation: Neither an advance fee agreement nor a minimum elapsed period appears among the conditions.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Outcome not reliably estimable
questions.stem: At 31 March the outcome of Sabarmati Projects Ltd's ₹700 lakh contract cannot be estimated reliably because a statutory clearance is still awaited. Costs of ₹260 lakh have been incurred, of which the recovery of only ₹230 lakh is probable. For the year the enterprise should recognise:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — revenue limited to recoverable costs incurred; costs expensed as incurred

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

options.text: Contract revenue of ₹260 lakh and contract costs of ₹260 lakh, showing neither profit nor loss
options.explanation: Revenue is capped at the costs whose recovery is PROBABLE, not at every cost incurred; recognising ₹260 lakh would recognise revenue for the ₹30 lakh that is not expected to be recovered.

options.text: No revenue at all, and the whole ₹260 lakh as an expense
options.explanation: AS 7 requires zero profit here, not necessarily zero revenue — the ₹230 lakh of probably recoverable cost is recognised as contract revenue.

options.text: Contract revenue of ₹230 lakh, with the unrecoverable ₹30 lakh carried forward as contract work in progress
options.explanation: Only costs relating to FUTURE activity whose recovery is probable may be carried as an asset; a cost whose recovery is not probable is expensed at once.

options.text: Contract revenue of ₹230 lakh, and the whole ₹260 lakh of contract costs as an expense
options.explanation: Correct. Revenue is recognised only to the extent of contract costs incurred whose recovery is probable — ₹230 lakh — while all contract costs incurred are expensed in the period, producing a ₹30 lakh loss and no profit.

questions.stem: Chambal Constructions Ltd's fixed price contract of ₹800 lakh has absorbed ₹360 lakh of cost so far, and a further ₹540 lakh is expected to be needed to complete it. The expected loss to be recognised as an expense in the current year is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — the entire expected loss is expensed immediately, whatever the stage

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

options.text: ₹60 lakh
options.explanation: ₹60 lakh is only the additional provision needed on top of the ₹40 lakh of loss that this year's revenue of ₹320 lakh less costs of ₹360 lakh already carries; the loss RECOGNISED for the year is the full ₹100 lakh.

options.text: Nil — the loss is recognised only as it is actually incurred in later years
options.explanation: Deferring a foreseeable loss is exactly what the AS 7 rule forbids.

options.text: ₹100 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Total expected cost 360 + 540 = ₹900 lakh against contract revenue of ₹800 lakh, so the expected loss of ₹100 lakh is recognised as an expense immediately and in full, irrespective of the stage of completion.

options.text: ₹40 lakh
options.explanation: This applies the 40% stage of completion (360/900) to the ₹100 lakh loss. The loss rule deliberately ignores the stage — the whole loss is expensed at once under prudence.

questions.stem: Tungabhadra Infra Ltd's contract price is ₹1,000 lakh. Costs incurred to date are ₹450 lakh, which includes ₹50 lakh of materials delivered to the site but not yet used; the estimated cost to complete is ₹400 lakh and already allows for consuming those materials. On the cost-to-cost basis, contract revenue for the period is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — costs relating to future activity excluded from costs to date

readLink.label: Read: Measuring the stage of completion, §1 →

options.text: ₹500 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Costs for work performed = 450 − 50 = ₹400 lakh; estimated total contract cost = 400 + 400 = ₹800 lakh; stage = 400/800 = 50%; contract revenue = 1,000 × 50% = ₹500 lakh.
This leaves the ₹50 lakh of unused site materials in the numerator (450/800 = 56.25%). Costs relating to future activity are excluded from costs to date and carried as an asset.

options.text: ₹450 lakh
options.explanation: This equates revenue with the costs incurred — the rule for contracts whose outcome is NOT reliably estimable, not the percentage of completion method.

options.text: ₹400 lakh
options.explanation: This reports the cost of work performed as the revenue; revenue is the contract price multiplied by the stage of completion.

questions.stem: A contractor is 40% complete on the cost-to-cost basis, has raised progress billings for 60% of the contract price, and holds a customer advance of ₹50 lakh. Contract revenue for the period is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — progress payments and advances are not measures of the stage of completion

readLink.label: Read: Measuring the stage of completion, §1 →

options.text: 60% of contract revenue, because billing evidences the customer's acceptance of the work
options.explanation: A running account bill is a demand for payment, not a certificate that 60% of the work has been performed; where surveys are the chosen measure, it is the surveyor's certification that counts.

options.text: 40% of contract revenue — progress payments and advances received often do not reflect the work performed and are no measure of the stage of completion
options.explanation: Correct. The stage measures permitted are the cost proportion, surveys of work performed and completion of a physical proportion; cash collected and amounts billed are none of them.

options.text: 60% of contract revenue, matching the progress billings raised
options.explanation: Billing is not earning; the excess of billings over the revenue recognised sits in the amount due TO customers.

options.text: 40% of contract revenue plus the ₹50 lakh advance received
options.explanation: An advance is money received before the related work is performed — a liability, not revenue.

questions.stem: In year 2 a contractor revises upwards its estimate of the total costs of a contract that is still profitable. Under AS 7 the revision is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — revisions are changes in accounting estimates under AS 5

readLink.label: Read: Changes in estimates, §1 →

options.text: A change in accounting policy, requiring disclosure of the effect on earlier years
options.explanation: The measurement basis — percentage of completion — has not changed at all; only the estimates fed into it have.

options.text: Ignored until the contract is completed, when the total profit is trued up
options.explanation: Percentage of completion is applied to CURRENT estimates at each reporting date, so a revision is reflected as soon as it is made.

options.text: A change in an accounting estimate under AS 5 — percentage of completion is applied cumulatively to the current estimates, so the effect falls on the current and future periods with no restatement of year 1
options.explanation: Correct. The cumulative catch-up in year 2 absorbs the revision; AS 5 treats changes in estimates prospectively.

options.text: A prior period item, because year 1's revenue was computed on an estimate now known to be wrong
options.explanation: A prior period item arises from an error or omission, not from an estimate that later turns out differently on new information.

questions.stem: Under AS 9, revenue is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — definition of revenue and its three sources

readLink.label: Read: What counts as revenue, §2 →

options.text: The net inflow remaining after deducting the cost of goods sold and the cost of rendering services
options.explanation: Revenue is a gross concept; the related costs are matched against it separately, and netting them would turn revenue into profit.

options.text: Every increase in economic benefit during the period, including gains on selling fixed assets and foreign exchange gains
options.explanation: Those gains fall outside the AS 9 definition, which is confined to inflows from ordinary activities in the three listed streams.

options.text: Only the amounts actually collected in cash during the period
options.explanation: Receivables and other consideration are revenue too — AS 9 fixes the timing of recognition on an accrual basis, not on collection.

options.text: The gross inflow of cash, receivables or other consideration arising in the course of an enterprise's ordinary activities from selling goods, rendering services and letting others use its resources for interest, royalties and dividends
options.explanation: Correct. Three features do the work: gross (not net of cost), arising from ORDINARY activities, and confined to the three listed sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT dealt with by AS 9?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — streams excluded from AS 9 because of special considerations

readLink.label: Read: What counts as revenue, §2 →

options.text: Royalty income from licensing a patent
options.explanation: Royalties are one of the three revenue streams AS 9 governs, recognised on an accrual basis per the terms of the agreement.

options.text: Revenue from repair services rendered to customers
options.explanation: The rendering of services is one of the three streams AS 9 governs.

options.text: Revenue arising from construction contracts
options.explanation: Correct. Construction contracts are left to AS 7; the other excluded streams are hire-purchase and lease agreements, government grants and other similar subsidies, and the revenue of insurance companies from insurance contracts.

options.text: Revenue from the sale of goods on instalment payment terms
options.explanation: An ordinary sale settled in instalments is squarely within AS 9 — the instalment terms alone do not delay recognition.

questions.stem: On the same day Konark Motors Ltd, a car maker, sells a used machine from its own workshop at a gain of ₹3,00,000, and Konark Realty Ltd, a dealer in land, sells a plot from its stock for ₹80,00,000. Under AS 9:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — 'ordinary activities' sorts revenue from disposal gains

readLink.label: Read: What counts as revenue, §2 →

options.text: Konark Motors recognises ₹3,00,000 as revenue and Konark Realty recognises only its margin on the plot
options.explanation: This inverts both answers: the disposal gain is not revenue, and a dealer's revenue is the whole sale price of its stock, not the margin.

options.text: Neither recognises revenue, because both transactions are disposals of assets
options.explanation: For a dealer in land, a plot is inventory rather than a non-current asset, so its sale is ordinary revenue.

options.text: Konark Motors recognises no revenue, only a gain on disposal, while Konark Realty recognises ₹80,00,000 as revenue
options.explanation: Correct. The plot is the dealer's stock-in-trade, so the whole sale price is revenue of its ordinary activities; the machine is the manufacturer's fixed asset, so its disposal produces a gain, not revenue.

options.text: Both recognise revenue — ₹3,00,000 and ₹80,00,000 respectively
options.explanation: Selling a used machine is not part of a car maker's ordinary activities, so no revenue arises — only a gain or loss on disposal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is revenue within the meaning of AS 9?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — items expressly outside the definition of revenue

readLink.label: Read: What counts as revenue, §2 →

options.text: The invoiced price of goods sold in the ordinary course of business
options.explanation: Correct. It is a gross inflow of consideration from an ordinary activity — the sale of goods.

options.text: An unrealised gain on restating a foreign currency loan at the closing rate
options.explanation: Realised and unrealised foreign exchange gains are expressly outside the AS 9 definition of revenue.

options.text: The natural increase in a dairy farm's herd during the year
options.explanation: Natural increases in herds and in agricultural and forest products are outside the definition.

options.text: A gain from discharging a loan at less than its carrying amount
options.explanation: Gains from the discharge of an obligation at less than its carrying amount are outside the definition.

questions.stem: Deccan Travels Ltd buys 200 seats outright on a charter flight, bears the loss on any seat it cannot sell, and resells them to travellers. Under AS 9 its revenue is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — principal vs agent turns on who bears the risks and rewards

readLink.label: Read: Agents earn commission, principals earn the price, §2 →

options.text: Only the service fee shown separately on each ticket
options.explanation: That is how an AGENT would account — but Deccan has taken the risk of unsold seats, which an agent does not.

options.text: Nil — an entity dealing in another party's services never recognises revenue, only a commission
options.explanation: Commission-only measurement applies where the entity merely arranges for another party to provide the goods or services; here it has bought the seats on its own account.

options.text: The gross amount charged to the travellers, because bearing the risk of unsold seats makes Deccan a principal
options.explanation: Correct. The test is who bears the risks and rewards: an entity that must itself provide the goods or services, or has taken the inventory risk, is a principal and recognises the gross amount.

options.text: Only its mark-up over the price paid to the airline, because the airline actually operates the flight
options.explanation: A principal's revenue is the gross amount charged; the price paid to the airline is its cost, not a netting adjustment.

questions.stem: Anantha Foods Online Ltd runs a delivery platform on which partner restaurants supply the food and bear the risks and rewards in it. In March the platform collected ₹9,60,000 from customers, made up of ₹7,20,000 charged by the restaurants, ₹1,80,000 of delivery charges levied by the platform, and ₹60,000 of GST collected on behalf of the government. The platform's revenue for March is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — agency revenue is the commission; indirect taxes collected are a liability

readLink.label: Read: Agents earn commission, principals earn the price, §2 →

options.explanation: This records the entire collection as revenue, although ₹7,20,000 belongs to the principals and ₹60,000 to the government.
This strips out only the GST and still treats the restaurants' ₹7,20,000 as the platform's own revenue.
This adds the ₹60,000 of GST to the delivery charge; an indirect tax collected on behalf of the government is nobody's revenue.

Correct. The platform merely arranges for the restaurants to supply the food, so it is an agent: its revenue is its own ₹1,80,000 delivery charge. The ₹7,20,000 is the restaurants' revenue and the ₹60,000 GST is a liability payable to government.

questions.stem: Revenue from the sale of goods is recognised under AS 9 when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — the two recognition conditions and the collectability proviso

readLink.label: Read: Sale of goods: the performance test, §2 →

options.text: The customer has paid, wholly or in part
options.explanation: Collection is not the trigger; only significant uncertainty about the amount of consideration or about ultimate collection can hold recognition back.

options.text: The seller has transferred property in the goods for a price, or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have passed with no effective control retained, AND no significant uncertainty exists about the amount of the consideration
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs must hold, and the whole recognition is subject to the proviso that at the time of performance it is not unreasonable to expect ultimate collection.

options.text: The goods have been physically despatched from the seller's premises
options.explanation: Despatch is evidence, not the test — a seller who keeps the significant risks in transit has not yet performed.

options.text: The invoice has been raised and entered in the sales day book
options.explanation: Raising an invoice is a book-keeping act; it cannot transfer property, risks or rewards.

questions.stem: Vaigai Exports Ltd despatched goods on 27 March. Under the contract legal title passes only when the goods reach the buyer's port in April, and Vaigai has taken the marine insurance in its own favour. At 31 March, Vaigai should:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — where property and risk diverge, revenue follows the risks and rewards

readLink.label: Read: Sale of goods: the performance test, §2 →

options.text: Recognise no revenue — it has retained the significant risks of ownership, so revenue waits until the goods reach the buyer
options.explanation: Correct. Where the transfer of property and the transfer of significant risks and rewards do not coincide, revenue follows the risks and rewards — and insuring the transit in its own favour shows Vaigai still carries them.

options.text: Recognise the revenue on despatch, because performance is complete once the goods leave the seller's premises
options.explanation: Leaving the premises transfers neither property nor risk here; both are contractually held back until arrival.

options.text: Recognise the revenue in proportion to the voyage completed by 31 March
options.explanation: Proportionate recognition belongs to the rendering of services; a sale of goods is recognised at a point, not spread over delivery.

options.text: Recognise the revenue and make a provision for a possible loss in transit
options.explanation: Providing for the risk concedes that the risk has not passed — the answer is to withhold recognition, not to recognise and provide.

questions.stem: Goods invoiced on 29 March remain in the seller's warehouse because the buyer has asked for delivery in April. Revenue may be recognised at 31 March only if:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — the three conditions for delivery delayed at the buyer's request

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.text: The goods are covered by insurance taken in the buyer's name
options.explanation: Insurance in the buyer's name is useful evidence but is not one of the three conditions.

options.text: The seller charges the buyer storage rent for the period of the delay
options.explanation: Storage rent, if any, is a separate service charge; it is not a condition for recognising the sale.

options.text: The goods are specifically identified and ready for delivery to the buyer, the delay is at the buyer's request, and the goods are no longer usable for another customer
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions must hold together before a bill-and-hold sale is treated as complete.

options.text: The buyer has paid at least a part of the price
options.explanation: Part payment is neither necessary nor sufficient; the three bill-and-hold conditions say nothing about collection.

questions.stem: Under a sale on approval or return, revenue is recognised when:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — acceptance, an adopting act, or lapse of the rejection period

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.text: Only on the buyer's written acceptance — an act adopting the transaction is not sufficient
options.explanation: An act adopting the transaction, such as reselling or pledging the goods, is expressly enough.

options.text: At the reporting date, for whatever proportion of such goods buyers usually retain
options.explanation: Past retention rates are not a recognition basis; each lot is judged by acceptance, adopting act or lapse of the rejection period.

options.text: The buyer formally accepts the goods, or does an act adopting the transaction, or the time fixed for rejection lapses (or a reasonable time, where none is fixed)
options.explanation: Correct. Any one of the three events completes the sale.

options.text: The goods are despatched to the buyer, since the buyer can always return them
options.explanation: Despatch on approval leaves the goods unsold — they remain the seller's inventory until acceptance or lapse.

questions.stem: Kaveri Appliances Ltd sent goods on sale or return during March at a selling price of ₹6,00,000, each lot carrying a 30-day approval period. By 31 March customers had formally accepted goods of ₹3,50,000; for goods of ₹1,50,000 the 30 days had run out with no rejection; and the balance of ₹1,00,000, despatched on 25 March, was still within the approval period with no response. Revenue for March is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — sale-or-return cut-off at the reporting date

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.explanation: This recognises the ₹1,00,000 still within its approval period and omits the ₹1,50,000 whose period has already lapsed — precisely the wrong way round.

Correct. ₹3,50,000 formally accepted + ₹1,50,000 on which the rejection period lapsed without rejection = ₹5,00,000; the ₹1,00,000 still inside its approval period is not yet a sale and stays in inventory.
This counts only the formal acceptances; the lapse of the fixed rejection period completes the sale just as acceptance does.
This treats despatch as the sale — goods on approval remain unsold until acceptance, an adopting act, or lapse of the rejection period.

questions.stem: Which statement about goods sold subject to installation is correct under AS 9?
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — complex vs simple installation; separately charged installation fee

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.text: Revenue on the goods is always recognised on delivery, installation being a separate service
options.explanation: Where the installation is complex and significant to using the goods, the buyer cannot use them until it is done, so revenue waits.

options.text: A separately charged installation fee is added to the sale value of the goods and recognised along with them
options.explanation: A separately charged fee is service revenue, recognised when the installation is complete — not merged into the goods revenue.

options.text: Where installation is complex and significant to the use of the goods, revenue waits for its satisfactory completion; where it is simple, revenue is recognised on the buyer's agreement to purchase, and a separately charged installation fee is service revenue recognised when the installation is complete
options.explanation: Correct. The significance of the installation to using the goods decides the timing of the goods revenue, and a separate installation fee is a service in its own right.

options.text: Revenue on the goods is always deferred until installation is complete
options.explanation: A simple installation — plugging in a refrigerator — does not hold back the sale.

questions.stem: Chenab Steel Ltd sells inventory to a financier for ₹90 lakh on 1 January under a firm agreement to buy it back on 30 June for ₹94.5 lakh. Under AS 9 Chenab should:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — sale and repurchase agreements are financing arrangements

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.text: Recognise revenue of ₹90 lakh in January and a purchase of ₹94.5 lakh in June
options.explanation: That reports a sale and a purchase where the substance is a loan against inventory — and it inflates both revenue and purchases.

options.text: Recognise revenue of ₹90 lakh and provide ₹4.5 lakh for the repurchase commitment
options.explanation: Providing for the commitment concedes that the goods are coming back; the transaction is not a sale in the first place.

options.text: Recognise no revenue, and treat the ₹4.5 lakh excess as an addition to the cost of the inventory on repurchase
options.explanation: The first half is right but the second is not — the excess is the cost of the finance, charged as interest expense, not capitalised into inventory.

options.text: Recognise no revenue and record a borrowing of ₹90 lakh, treating the ₹4.5 lakh excess as interest expense
options.explanation: Correct. A sale coupled with an agreement to repurchase the same goods is a financing arrangement in substance; the inventory never leaves Chenab's balance sheet and the excess of the repurchase price over the sale price is interest.

questions.stem: Godavari Ceramics Ltd sent goods costing ₹4,00,000 to a consignee at a pro-forma invoice price of ₹5,00,000. By 31 March the consignee had sold three-fourths of the goods to customers for ₹4,80,000 and remitted the proceeds after deducting commission of ₹24,000. Godavari's revenue from the consignment is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — consignment revenue arises only on the sale to a third party

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.explanation: Correct. The consignee holds the goods on Godavari's behalf, so revenue arises only when they are sold to third parties: ₹4,80,000. The commission is Godavari's expense, and the unsold one-fourth (cost ₹1,00,000) remains its inventory.
This takes the pro-forma invoice value of everything despatched; despatch to a consignee is not a sale, and one-fourth of the goods is still unsold.
This reports the sale net of the ₹24,000 commission; the commission is an expense of selling, not a deduction in arriving at revenue.
This takes three-fourths of the ₹5,00,000 pro-forma price; revenue is the amount at which the consignee actually sold the goods to customers.

questions.stem: Krishna Textiles Ltd invoiced gross sales of ₹25,00,000 during the year, allowing a trade discount of 6% on the invoices and a volume rebate of ₹40,000 to one dealer; customers paying within fifteen days took cash discounts totalling ₹18,000. Revenue for the year is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — trade discounts and volume rebates reduce revenue; cash discounts are an expense

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

options.explanation: This also deducts the ₹18,000 cash discount. Revenue stays at the gross amount and the cash discount is treated as an expense when the customer pays net.
This deducts the 6% trade discount but leaves the ₹40,000 volume rebate in revenue; volume rebates are deducted in determining revenue exactly as trade discounts are.
This reports the gross invoiced amount, deducting neither the trade discount nor the rebate.
Correct. 25,00,000 − 1,50,000 trade discount (6% of 25,00,000) − 40,000 volume rebate = ₹23,10,000; the ₹18,000 cash discount is the cost of collecting early and is charged as an expense.

questions.stem: Kosi Engineers Ltd has two engagements: installing one machine, a single act; and an annual maintenance contract for twelve machines requiring four service visits during the year. Under AS 9:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — completed service contract vs proportionate completion

readLink.label: Read: Rendering of services, §2 →

options.text: The installation is recognised on the completed service contract method when the installation is done, while the maintenance contract is recognised by proportionate completion as the visits are performed
options.explanation: Correct. The completed service contract method fits performance consisting of a single act (or where the unperformed acts are so significant that performance is incomplete); the proportionate completion method fits performance consisting of more than one act.

options.text: Both engagements are recognised by the proportionate completion method
options.explanation: A single act cannot be split into proportions — there is only one act to perform, so revenue waits for it.

options.text: Both engagements are recognised only when the whole engagement is complete
options.explanation: The maintenance contract consists of more than one act, so revenue follows each visit as it is performed.

options.text: The installation is recognised in proportion to the time spent on it, and the maintenance fee when the annual contract expires
options.explanation: This reverses both treatments — the single act goes to completed service, and the multi-act contract goes to proportionate completion.

questions.stem: Narmada Finance Ltd invested ₹24,00,000 in the 12% bonds of another company on 1 August 20X1. Interest is payable annually on 30 June, so nothing had been received by 31 March 20X2, and there is no uncertainty about collection. Interest income for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — interest accrues on a time proportion basis

readLink.label: Read: Interest, royalties and dividends, §2 →

options.explanation: Correct. Interest is recognised on a time proportion basis on the amount outstanding at the applicable rate: 24,00,000 × 12% × 8/12 (1 August to 31 March) = ₹1,92,000.
This charges a full twelve months' interest although the bonds were held for only eight months of the year.
This counts nine months from 1 July, the start of the bonds' own interest year, instead of the eight months since the investment was made.

options.text: Nil
options.explanation: This waits for the 30 June coupon; interest accrues by time, and collection — about which there is no uncertainty here — is not the trigger.

questions.stem: Kalinga Publishers Ltd licensed a title for a royalty of 5% of the licensee's net sales, settled half-yearly. The licensee's audited net sales for the year ended 31 March 20X2 were ₹90,00,000, and ₹2,10,000 of royalty had reached Kalinga by 31 March; there is no uncertainty about the balance. Royalty income for the year is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — royalties accrue per the terms of the agreement

readLink.label: Read: Interest, royalties and dividends, §2 →

options.explanation: This recognises only the royalty collected in cash, turning an accrual basis into a receipts basis.
This recognises only the unreceived balance and drops the ₹2,10,000 already collected during the year.

options.text: Nil
options.explanation: This defers the whole royalty to the next half-yearly settlement; with no uncertainty about collection, the accrued royalty is revenue of this year.
Correct. Royalties are recognised on an accrual basis in accordance with the terms of the agreement: 5% × 90,00,000 = ₹4,50,000, of which ₹2,40,000 stands receivable at the year end.

questions.stem: Explain the percentage of completion method under AS 7 and state the conditions that must be satisfied before the outcome of (a) a fixed price contract and (b) a cost-plus contract can be estimated reliably. What is the treatment when the outcome cannot be estimated reliably? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Percentage of completion: contract revenue and contract costs are recognised by reference to the stage of completion at the reporting date, so that each period reports the revenue, expenses and profit of the work performed in it; the method is applied on a cumulative basis to the current estimates of contract revenue and contract costs

Fixed price contract — all four: total contract revenue can be measured reliably; it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to the enterprise; both the contract costs to complete and the stage of completion at the reporting date can be measured reliably; and the contract costs attributable to the contract are clearly identifiable and reliably measurable so that actual costs can be compared with prior estimates

Cost-plus contract — only two: it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to the enterprise; and the contract costs attributable to the contract, whether or not specifically reimbursable, are clearly identifiable and can be measured reliably

Outcome not reliably estimable: recognise revenue only to the extent of contract costs incurred whose recovery is probable, and recognise contract costs as an expense in the period incurred — no profit; apply percentage of completion once the uncertainties are resolved

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Contract revenue and contract costs
questions.stem: State the items that make up contract revenue and contract costs under AS 7, including the costs that are expressly excluded. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Contract revenue: the initial amount of revenue agreed in the contract, plus variations, claims and incentive payments to the extent that it is probable they will result in revenue and they are capable of being reliably measured; agreed cost escalations are added and penalties for delay are deducted

Direct costs: site labour including supervision, materials used, depreciation of plant used on the contract, costs of moving plant and materials to and from the site, hire of plant, contract-specific design and technical assistance, estimated rectification and guarantee work including expected warranty costs, and third-party claims — reduced by incidental income not forming part of contract revenue, such as the sale of surplus materials or of plant at the end of the contract

Allocable costs attributable to contract activity in general, allocated systematically and rationally on normal levels of construction activity: insurance, design not related to a specific contract, construction overheads, and borrowing costs under AS 16; plus other costs specifically chargeable to the customer under the terms of the contract

Excluded: general administration costs and research and development costs for which reimbursement is not specified in the contract, selling costs, and depreciation of idle plant not used on a particular contract; costs relating to future activity (for example materials delivered but not yet used) are excluded from costs to date and carried as an asset where recovery is probable

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Losses, uncertainty and estimate revisions
questions.stem: How does AS 7 deal with (i) an expected loss on a contract, (ii) an amount already recognised as contract revenue that later becomes doubtful of collection, and (iii) a revision in the estimates of contract revenue or contract costs? Illustrate (i) briefly. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Expected loss: when total contract costs are expected to exceed total contract revenue, the entire expected loss is recognised as an expense immediately, irrespective of the stage of completion, whether or not work has commenced and regardless of the profit expected on other contracts

Illustration: contract revenue ₹800 lakh, costs incurred ₹360 lakh and further costs ₹540 lakh — total expected cost ₹900 lakh, expected loss ₹100 lakh recognised in full now; at a 40% stage the year's revenue of ₹320 lakh less costs of ₹360 lakh already carries ₹40 lakh, so a provision of ₹60 lakh completes the charge

Revenue already recognised that becomes doubtful of collection: the uncollectable amount is recognised as an expense (or a provision), and is NOT treated as an adjustment of the amount of contract revenue already recognised

Revision of estimates: percentage of completion is applied on a cumulative basis to the current estimates each period, so a revision of contract revenue, contract costs or the outcome is a change in an accounting estimate under AS 5 — it affects the current and future periods and no earlier period is restated

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Segmenting, combining and additional assets
questions.stem: When may a single construction contract be segmented into separate contracts, and when must several contracts be combined into one? How is an additional asset ordered by the customer treated? (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Segmenting — all three conditions: separate proposals were submitted for each asset; each asset was subject to separate negotiation with the contractor and the customer free to accept or reject that part; and the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified

Combining (whether with one customer or several) — all three conditions: the group of contracts was negotiated as a single package; the contracts are so closely interrelated that they are in effect part of a single project with an overall profit margin; and they are performed concurrently or in a continuous sequence

Additional asset: treated as a separate construction contract when EITHER it differs significantly in design, technology or function from the asset or assets covered by the original contract, OR its price is negotiated without regard to the original contract price

questions.stem: State the disclosure requirements of AS 7, define retentions, progress billings and advances, and explain how the amount due from or to customers for contract work is computed. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: General disclosures: the amount of contract revenue recognised in the period; the methods used to determine the contract revenue recognised; and the methods used to determine the stage of completion of contracts in progress

For contracts in progress at the reporting date: the aggregate amount of costs incurred and recognised profits (less recognised losses) up to the reporting date; the amount of advances received; and the amount of retentions

Definitions: retentions are amounts of progress billings not paid until the satisfaction of conditions specified in the contract or until defects have been rectified; progress billings are amounts billed for work performed on a contract whether or not they have been paid by the customer; advances are amounts received by the contractor before the related work is performed

Net position per contract = costs incurred + recognised profits − recognised losses − progress billings; a positive figure is disclosed as the gross amount due FROM customers (an asset) and a negative figure as the gross amount due TO customers (a liability)

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 9 · Revenue and the sale of goods
questions.stem: Define revenue under AS 9, state the transactions it covers and the streams excluded from its scope, and set out the conditions for recognising revenue from the sale of goods. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Revenue is the gross inflow of cash, receivables or other consideration arising in the course of the ordinary activities of an enterprise; where an agency relationship exists, revenue is the amount of commission and not the gross inflow
Covered: revenue from the sale of goods, from the rendering of services, and from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest, royalties and dividends

Excluded because of special considerations: revenue arising from construction contracts, from hire-purchase and lease agreements, from government grants and other similar subsidies, and the revenue of insurance companies from insurance contracts; also outside the definition are realised and unrealised gains on non-current assets, unrealised holding gains on current assets, natural increases in herds and agricultural and forest products, foreign exchange gains, and gains on discharging or restating an obligation

Sale of goods: recognise when the seller has transferred to the buyer the property in the goods for a price, or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred and the seller retains no effective control of the goods to a degree usually associated with ownership; AND no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration — subject throughout to the proviso that at the time of performance it is not unreasonable to expect ultimate collection

questions.stem: Explain the AS 9 treatment of each of the following: (i) delivery delayed at the buyer's request; (ii) sale on approval; (iii) goods sold subject to installation; (iv) sale and repurchase agreements; (v) consignment sales; and (vi) trade discounts as against cash discounts. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Delivery delayed at the buyer's request (bill and hold): the sale is complete, though the goods are still with the seller, when the goods are specifically identified and ready for delivery, the delay is at the buyer's request, and the goods are not usable for another customer

Sale on approval: no revenue until the buyer formally accepts the goods, does an act adopting the transaction, or the time fixed for rejection lapses — or, where no time is fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed

Goods sold subject to installation: where installation is complex and significant to the use of the goods, revenue waits for its satisfactory completion; where it is simple, revenue is recognised on the buyer's agreement to purchase; a separately charged installation fee is service revenue recognised when the installation is complete

Sale and repurchase agreements: a sale coupled with an agreement to repurchase the same goods later is a financing arrangement — recognise a borrowing rather than revenue, and treat the excess of the repurchase price over the sale price as interest

Consignment sales: the consignee holds the goods on the consignor's behalf, so no revenue arises until the goods are sold to a third party; unsold consignment stock remains the consignor's closing inventory

Trade discounts and volume rebates are deducted in determining revenue; cash discounts are different — revenue is recorded at the gross amount and the discount allowed for early payment is charged as an expense

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 9 · Uncertainty, interest, royalties and dividends
questions.stem: Explain how AS 9 deals with uncertainty about the collection of revenue, and state the bases on which revenue from interest, royalties and dividends is recognised. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Uncertainty existing at the time of raising the claim — price escalations, export incentives or penal interest with a poor record of recovery: postpone recognition to the extent of the uncertainty and recognise the revenue only in the period in which it becomes reasonably certain; the later recognition is neither a prior period item nor an extraordinary item
Uncertainty arising AFTER revenue has been recognised: make a separate provision for the doubtful amount (or write off the bad debt) — do not adjust the revenue originally recorded

Interest, royalties and dividends are recognised only when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists: interest on a time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and the rate applicable; royalties on an accrual basis in accordance with the terms of the relevant agreement; dividends when the owner's right to receive payment is established, that is on declaration
Instalment payment terms alone never delay recognition where there is no uncertainty about collection; revenue is the whole consideration, with any interest element accounted for separately
Disclosure: an enterprise discloses the circumstances in which revenue recognition has been postponed pending the resolution of significant uncertainties

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Case: Vindhya Infrastructure (three-year percentage of completion)
questions.case: Vindhya Infrastructure Ltd began a fixed price contract of ₹2,000 lakh for a bypass on 1 April 20X1. The outcome of the contract could be estimated reliably throughout, and Vindhya measures the stage of completion on the cost-to-cost basis. Year 1 (ended 31 March 20X2): costs incurred ₹400 lakh, estimated further costs to complete ₹1,200 lakh. Year 2 (ended 31 March 20X3): costs incurred to date ₹960 lakh, estimated further costs to complete ₹640 lakh. Year 3 (ended 31 March 20X4): the bypass was handed over, the total cost actually incurred over the three years being ₹1,650 lakh.

readLink.label: Read: The percentage of completion method, §1 →

questions.stem: Contract revenue for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — stage of completion on the cost-to-cost basis

options.text: Nil — revenue is recognised only when the bypass is handed over
options.explanation: That is the completed contract method, which AS 7 does not permit once the outcome can be estimated reliably.

options.text: ₹500 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Estimated total cost = 400 + 1,200 = ₹1,600 lakh; stage = 400/1,600 = 25%; contract revenue = 2,000 × 25% = ₹500 lakh.

options.text: ₹400 lakh
options.explanation: This measures the stage against the contract PRICE (400/2,000 = 20%) instead of the estimated total COST — or simply reports the costs incurred as revenue.

options.text: ₹100 lakh
options.explanation: ₹100 lakh is the year's profit, not its revenue; revenue is the contract price times the stage of completion.

questions.stem: Profit recognised for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — revenue less contract costs of reaching the stage

options.text: ₹100 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Revenue ₹500 lakh less contract costs of the work performed ₹400 lakh = ₹100 lakh — which is also 25% of the ₹400 lakh total expected profit (2,000 − 1,600).

options.text: ₹400 lakh
options.explanation: This recognises the whole expected contract profit of ₹400 lakh at once; only a LOSS is recognised in full immediately — profit follows the stage of completion.

options.text: ₹500 lakh
options.explanation: This treats the whole year-1 revenue as profit and never charges the ₹400 lakh of contract costs against it.

options.text: Nil
options.explanation: Deferring all profit to completion is the completed contract method, which AS 7 does not permit here.

questions.stem: Contract revenue for the year ended 31 March 20X3 (that year alone) is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — cumulative application, current-period figure by difference

options.text: ₹700 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Estimated total cost = 960 + 640 = ₹1,600 lakh; stage = 960/1,600 = 60%; cumulative revenue = 2,000 × 60% = ₹1,200 lakh; less ₹500 lakh recognised in year 1 = ₹700 lakh for year 2.

options.text: ₹1,200 lakh
options.explanation: ₹1,200 lakh is the CUMULATIVE revenue to 31 March 20X3; the year's figure is arrived at after deducting the ₹500 lakh already recognised.

options.text: ₹560 lakh
options.explanation: ₹560 lakh (960 − 400) is the contract cost of year 2, not its revenue.

options.text: ₹900 lakh
options.explanation: This applies the 60% stage to the ₹1,500 lakh of contract price not yet recognised; the stage applies to the whole contract price on a cumulative basis.

questions.stem: Profit recognised for the year ended 31 March 20X4 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — final-year profit as total profit less profit already recognised

options.text: ₹110 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Total contract profit = 2,000 − 1,650 = ₹350 lakh; profit already recognised = 100 (year 1) + 140 (year 2: revenue 700 − costs 560) = ₹240 lakh; year-3 profit = 350 − 240 = ₹110 lakh, which equals revenue 800 (2,000 − 1,200) less costs 690 (1,650 − 960).

options.text: ₹350 lakh
options.explanation: ₹350 lakh is the profit of the whole contract; ₹240 lakh of it was already recognised in years 1 and 2.

options.text: ₹210 lakh
options.explanation: This deducts only the year-2 profit of ₹140 lakh from the total ₹350 lakh and forgets the ₹100 lakh recognised in year 1.

options.text: ₹140 lakh
options.explanation: ₹140 lakh is the year-2 profit (revenue 700 less costs 560), not the year-3 figure.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 7 · Case: Konkan Constructions (loss-making contract and the amount due to customers)
questions.case: Konkan Constructions Ltd holds a fixed price contract of ₹1,500 lakh to build a jetty over three years, and the outcome can be estimated reliably. At 31 March 20X2, the end of the first year, contract costs of ₹640 lakh have been incurred, of which ₹40 lakh is structural steel delivered to the site but not yet used; the estimated further cost to complete is ₹1,000 lakh, an estimate that already allows for consuming that steel. Progress billings of ₹700 lakh have been raised, of which ₹70 lakh is retention money not yet due for payment, and advances of ₹90 lakh have been received from the customer.

readLink.label: Read: Measuring the stage of completion, §1 →

questions.stem: For measuring the stage of completion, the contract costs to be taken as incurred for work performed to date are:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — costs relating to future activity excluded from costs to date

options.text: ₹640 lakh
options.explanation: This leaves the unused steel in the costs of work performed and would overstate the stage of completion.

options.text: ₹560 lakh
options.explanation: This deducts the ₹40 lakh twice — once from the costs incurred and again from the balance.

options.text: ₹680 lakh
options.explanation: This adds the ₹40 lakh of unused steel to the ₹640 lakh, although the ₹640 lakh already includes it.

options.text: ₹600 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. 640 − 40 = ₹600 lakh; the steel lying unused at the site relates to future activity, so it is excluded from costs to date and carried as an asset (contract work in progress) because its recovery is probable.

questions.stem: Contract revenue to be recognised for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — cost-to-cost stage applied to contract revenue

options.text: ₹600 lakh
options.explanation: This uses the unadjusted ₹640 lakh over the ₹1,600 lakh total (40%); the unused steel must first come out of the costs to date.

options.text: ₹640 lakh
options.explanation: This reports the costs incurred as the revenue, which is the rule for contracts whose outcome cannot be estimated reliably.
This applies the 62.5% NOT yet completed instead of the 37.5% completed.
Correct. Estimated total cost = 600 + 1,000 = ₹1,600 lakh; stage = 600/1,600 = 37.5%; contract revenue = 1,500 × 37.5% = ₹562.50 lakh.

questions.stem: The provision to be created at 31 March 20X2 for the expected loss on the contract is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — expected loss recognised in full, less the loss already carried in the year's result

options.text: ₹62.50 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Expected loss = 1,600 − 1,500 = ₹100 lakh, recognised in full at once. The year's own figures already carry ₹37.50 lakh of it (revenue 562.50 less costs 600), so a provision of ₹62.50 lakh tops the charge up to ₹100 lakh.

options.text: ₹100 lakh
options.explanation: This provides the whole expected loss again on top of the ₹37.50 lakh already reflected in the year's revenue-less-cost figures, charging ₹137.50 lakh in all.

options.text: ₹37.50 lakh
options.explanation: ₹37.50 lakh is the loss the year's own revenue and costs already show; the provision is the amount still needed to reach the full ₹100 lakh.

options.text: Nil — the loss is recognised as it arises in the remaining two years
options.explanation: AS 7 requires the entire expected loss to be recognised as an expense immediately, whatever the stage of completion.

questions.stem: Taking contract costs incurred for work performed to date, the amount to be presented for this contract at 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U1 — gross amount due from/to customers

options.text: ₹160 lakh due TO customers
options.explanation: This uses the ₹640 lakh of costs incurred including the unused steel (640 − 100 − 700); the steel is carried separately as an asset.

options.text: ₹100 lakh due TO customers
options.explanation: This omits the ₹100 lakh of recognised loss from the computation (600 − 700).

options.text: ₹200 lakh due TO customers, shown as a liability
options.explanation: Correct. Costs incurred 600 + recognised profits nil − recognised losses 100 − progress billings 700 = −₹200 lakh; a negative figure is the gross amount due to customers. The ₹90 lakh of advances is disclosed separately, and the ₹70 lakh retention is part of the billings already raised.

options.text: ₹200 lakh due FROM customers, shown as an asset
options.explanation: The sign is the wrong way round: billings of ₹700 lakh exceed costs less recognised losses, so the customer is ahead, not the contractor.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 9 · Case: Malabar Traders (four transactions at the year end)
questions.case: Malabar Traders Ltd is drawing up its accounts for the year ended 31 March 20X2. (i) Goods invoiced at ₹3,20,000 were sold on 28 March and are lying in Malabar's warehouse at the buyer's written request; they are specifically identified, are not usable for any other customer, and are ready for despatch. (ii) Goods with a selling price of ₹8,00,000 were sent to a consignee, of which the consignee had sold goods worth ₹5,60,000 to customers by 31 March. (iii) Goods of ₹4,00,000 were sold on 1 March on two months' approval; buyers had accepted ₹2,50,000 worth by 31 March and had neither accepted nor rejected the rest. (iv) Counter sales were invoiced at a gross ₹12,50,000 subject to a trade discount of 8%, and a machine used in Malabar's own godown was sold at a profit of ₹60,000.

readLink.label: Read: Timing in the classic scenarios, §2 →

questions.stem: The revenue Malabar should recognise on the consignment (item ii) is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — consignment revenue arises only on the onward sale

options.text: Nil until the consignee remits the sale proceeds
options.explanation: Recognition follows the onward sale to third parties, not the remittance of cash.
Correct. The consignee holds the goods on Malabar's behalf, so only the ₹5,60,000 sold onward to customers is revenue; the unsold ₹2,40,000 remains Malabar's closing inventory.
This treats the despatch to the consignee as a sale; the consignee is not a customer.
₹2,40,000 is the selling price of the goods still lying UNSOLD with the consignee.

questions.stem: The revenue Malabar should recognise on the approval sales (item iii) is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — sale on approval recognised on acceptance or lapse of the rejection period

options.text: Nil until the two-month approval period expires on 1 May 20X2
options.explanation: Formal acceptance completes the sale for the ₹2,50,000 without waiting for the period to run out.

Correct. Only the goods formally accepted by 31 March are sold; the two-month approval period on the balance ₹1,50,000 runs to 1 May 20X2, so those goods are still Malabar's inventory at the year end.
This recognises the whole despatch; goods on approval remain unsold until acceptance, an adopting act or lapse of the rejection period.
₹1,50,000 is the portion NOT yet accepted.

questions.stem: Item (i) and the sale of the godown machine should be dealt with as:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — bill and hold conditions; disposal of a fixed asset is not revenue

options.text: Defer both amounts to 20X2–X3
options.explanation: Neither should be deferred as revenue of the next year — the sale is complete, and the machine gain is never revenue.

options.text: Recognise ₹3,20,000 as revenue; the ₹60,000 on the machine is not revenue at all, only a gain on disposal
options.explanation: Correct. All three bill-and-hold conditions are met — the goods are specifically identified, not usable for another customer, ready for delivery, and the delay is at the buyer's request. Selling a machine used in the business is not an ordinary activity of a trading company.

options.text: Defer the ₹3,20,000 until the goods are despatched, and recognise the ₹60,000 as revenue
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: a bill-and-hold sale satisfying the three conditions is complete, and a disposal gain is not revenue.

options.text: Recognise both the ₹3,20,000 and the ₹60,000 as revenue
options.explanation: The ₹3,20,000 is right, but the gain on selling a fixed asset falls outside the AS 9 definition of revenue.

questions.stem: Total revenue for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — aggregating the four items on AS 9 principles

options.explanation: This takes the whole ₹4,00,000 of approval sales, adding the ₹1,50,000 on which no acceptance has yet come.
This adds the ₹60,000 gain on the godown machine, which is not revenue of a trading company's ordinary activities.

Correct. 3,20,000 (bill and hold) + 5,60,000 (consignment sold onward) + 2,50,000 (approvals received) + 11,50,000 (12,50,000 less the 8% trade discount of ₹1,00,000) = ₹22,80,000; the machine gain is excluded.
This takes the whole ₹8,00,000 consignment as revenue, adding the ₹2,40,000 still unsold with the consignee.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · AS 9 · Case: Nilgiri Estates (interest, royalty, dividend and a doubtful claim)
questions.case: Nilgiri Estates Ltd is finalising its accounts for the year ended 31 March 20X2. (i) It holds ₹30,00,000 of 10% bonds of another company, acquired on 1 October 20X1; interest is payable annually and collection is not in doubt. (ii) It has licensed its brand for a royalty of 4% of the licensee's net sales; the licensee's audited net sales for the year were ₹1,25,00,000, of which royalty of ₹2,00,000 had been received by 31 March, the balance being collectable without doubt. (iii) It holds 40,000 equity shares of an investee company that proposed a dividend of ₹5 per share on 12 May 20X2 for the year ended 31 March 20X2; the members declared the dividend at the annual general meeting on 8 August 20X2. (iv) In February 20X2 Nilgiri raised a price-escalation claim of ₹18,00,000 on a government department that has disputed similar claims in the past, so recovery was uncertain when the claim was raised; in August 20X2 the department accepted ₹11,00,000.

readLink.label: Read: Interest, royalties and dividends, §2 →

questions.stem: Interest income to be recognised for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — interest on a time proportion basis

options.explanation: This halves the six months' interest again, as though only a quarter of the year were involved.

options.text: Nil until the annual interest is actually received
options.explanation: Interest is recognised as it accrues by time; with no uncertainty about collection there is nothing to postpone.
Correct. Time proportion basis on the amount outstanding at the applicable rate: 30,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 (1 October to 31 March) = ₹1,50,000.
This takes a full year's interest although the bonds were held for only six months of the year.

questions.stem: Royalty income to be recognised for the year ended 31 March 20X2 is:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — royalties accrue in accordance with the terms of the agreement

options.explanation: Correct. 4% × 1,25,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 accrues under the agreement; ₹2,00,000 has been received and ₹3,00,000 stands as a receivable.
This recognises only the cash received, which is a receipts basis rather than the accrual basis the agreement's terms require.
This recognises only the amount still outstanding and drops the ₹2,00,000 already received.

options.text: Nil until the licensee settles the full year's royalty
options.explanation: There is no uncertainty as to measurability or collectability, so the whole accrued royalty is revenue of the year.

questions.stem: The dividend of ₹5 per share on the 40,000 shares should be recognised:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — dividends when the owner's right to receive payment is established

options.text: ₹2,00,000 in 20X1–X2, the year whose profits the dividend relates to
options.explanation: The year to which the investee's profits relate does not fix the investor's right; the right arises on declaration.

options.text: ₹2,00,000 in 20X1–X2, because the dividend was proposed before Nilgiri's accounts were approved
options.explanation: A proposal is only a recommendation by the investee's board; it can be reduced or refused by the members, so no right exists yet.

options.text: ₹2,00,000 in 20X2–X3, when the dividend warrant is actually received
options.explanation: The right is established on declaration, not on receipt of the money.

options.text: Not at all in 20X1–X2; ₹2,00,000 is recognised in 20X2–X3, the year in which the members declared the dividend
options.explanation: Correct. Dividends are recognised when the owner's right to receive payment is established — for a proposed dividend that is the date of declaration by the members, here 8 August 20X2.

questions.stem: The escalation claim of ₹18,00,000 should be dealt with as follows:
questions.sourceRef: SM Ch 8 U2 — uncertainty existing at the time of raising the claim

options.text: Recognise ₹11,00,000 in 20X1–X2 by restating that year's accounts as a prior period adjustment
options.explanation: The August 20X2 acceptance is new information about a claim that was rightly not recognised earlier, not the correction of an error — so no restatement and no prior period item.

options.text: Recognise nothing in 20X1–X2 because collection was uncertain when the claim was raised, and recognise ₹11,00,000 in 20X2–X3 when it became reasonably certain — not as a prior period item
options.explanation: Correct. Where the uncertainty exists at the time of raising the claim, recognition is postponed to the extent of the uncertainty; the amount is recognised in the period in which it becomes reasonably certain, and that later recognition is neither a prior period item nor an extraordinary item.

options.text: Recognise ₹18,00,000 in 20X1–X2 and write back ₹7,00,000 in 20X2–X3
options.explanation: Recognising revenue that is doubtful from the outset and reversing it later is exactly what the postponement rule prevents.

options.text: Recognise ₹18,00,000 in 20X1–X2 and make a provision of ₹7,00,000 against the receivable
options.explanation: The provision route applies where the uncertainty ARISES AFTER revenue has already been recognised; here the doubt existed when the claim was raised.
